steps.stepTitle: Scene 1: Scrambled Clues in the Vault
steps.settingDescription: The royal diamond is missing! Detective Ira finds four torn location notes—each ruined by a misplaced or swapped preposition.

dialogues.line: Look at clue one: 'Meet AT Sunday IN 5 o'clock BETWEEN all the five pillars!' And clue two: 'We discussed ABOUT the lock before entering INTO the room!'
No wonder you went to the wrong pillar! One wrong preposition flips place, time, and direction—and 'discuss' and 'enter (a room)' refuse prepositions altogether!
A Preposition always links to its Prepositional Object (a noun, object pronoun, or '-ing' gerund)—though in questions and relative clauses, the preposition may step neatly to the end!
Let us decode time, space, collocations, and end-positioned prepositions to recover Maharaj Vakya's diamond!

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Master prepositions of time/space/relation, prepositional objects, fixed collocations, and preposition position.

steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Prepositions of Time build an inverted pyramid: AT is the pinpoint tip (at 6 p.m., at noon), ON is a single calendar square (on Monday, on 15 August), and IN is the wide box around months, years, and seasons (in July, in 2026)!
steps.formalDefinition: A preposition shows the spatial, temporal, or logical relationship between its prepositional object (noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund) and another element in the clause. Core contrasts include at/on/in, since/for, by/until, between/among, beside/besides, and in/into.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Keep these five contrast pairs crystal clear:
1) Time Pyramid: AT (clock times, night, noon, dawn) • ON (days, dates, 'on Monday morning') • IN (months, seasons, years, 'in the morning'—remember ZERO preposition before 'today, tomorrow, yesterday, last/next/this + week'!).
2) Duration vs. Deadline: SINCE + starting point ('since 2019 / since Monday') vs. FOR + length of time ('for two hours'); BY = no later than ('Finish by 5 p.m.') vs. UNTIL = continuing up to ('Wait until 5 p.m.').
3) Space Pairs: BETWEEN (two, or distinct named items individually) vs. AMONG (3+ in a group); BESIDE (= next to) vs. BESIDES (= in addition to); IN (static location) vs. INTO (motion inward).
4) Prepositional Object Rule: Use objective pronouns ('for you and me') and gerunds ('tired of waiting', 'insist on paying', 'prevented me from going'—NEVER *to go!).
5) Zero-Preposition Verbs: Do NOT insert 'about/into/for' after 'discuss, order, enter (a room), resemble, marry, reach' (*discuss about → 'discuss the case').

structurePatterns.sample: at 7:30 a.m. • on Tuesday • in October • Ø next Friday (NOT *on next Friday)
interested in solving • good at drawing • between him and me

structurePatterns.formula: between (2) vs. among (3+) | beside (next to) vs. besides (apart from) | by (agent) vs. with (instrument)
structurePatterns.sample: The scroll was signed by Ira (agent) with a fountain pen (instrument).

realLifeExamples.sentence: Beside the brass lamp lay three clues; besides those, Ira found a glove.
The treaty was signed among the four coastal kingdoms in 1998.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'Among' fits four kingdoms; 'in' fits a year.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: We entered into the hall on yesterday and discussed about the problem since two hours.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: We entered the hall yesterday and discussed the problem for two hours.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: 'Enter (a place)' and 'discuss' take direct objects without prepositions; 'yesterday' takes no 'on'; duration 'two hours' takes 'for' (not 'since').

exceptions: Even with more than two items, use 'between' when showing clear one-to-one connections ('a railway link between Delhi, Jaipur, and Agra').
'Made of' (material stays visible: 'a ring made of gold') vs. 'made from' (material is transformed: 'paper made from bamboo').

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 1: Crack the Time & Place Clues
steps.storyPrompt: Detective Ira decodes a coded diary line: "The guard noticed the shadow ____ midnight ____ Thursday, and has been guarding the gate ____ three hours."
steps.questionPrompt: Pick the option that fills all three blanks accurately:
options: in / in / since
at / on / for
on / at / for
at / in / since
steps.hint: Midnight = pinpoint ('at'); Thursday = calendar day ('on'); three hours = length/duration ('for')!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Vault lock #1 opened! 'At midnight', 'on Thursday', and 'for three hours' match exact time rules."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use 'at' for midnight/noon/clock times, 'on' for weekdays, and 'for' for durations.

feedbackWrongByOption.at / in / since: Days take 'on' (not 'in'), and durations like 'three hours' take 'for' (not 'since').

steps.simplerExample: Meet at noon on Monday; wait for ten minutes.

steps.storyPrompt: Vaani examines the vault lock: "The secret latch was opened ____ Detective Ira ____ a thin silver hairpin."
steps.questionPrompt: Enter the two prepositions separated by ' / ' (agent, then instrument tool):
steps.sentenceTemplate: The secret latch was opened ________ Detective Ira ________ a thin silver hairpin.
steps.hint: Who did the action (agent)? Use 'by'. What tool/instrument did she use? Use 'with'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Vault lock #2 clicked open! 'By' marks the doer (agent), while 'with' marks the physical tool/instrument."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use 'by' before the person (agent) and 'with' before the tool (instrument).
steps.simplerExample: The letter was written by Riya with blue ink.

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Position of Prepositions & Fixed Collocations
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: A preposition usually sits IN FRONT of its object like a doorstep ('on the chair')—EXCEPT when its object escapes to the front of a Wh-question, a Relative Clause, or a Passive sentence, leaving the loyal preposition standing neatly at the END ('Which chair did you sit on?')!
steps.formalDefinition: Although a preposition normally precedes its complement inside a prepositional phrase, English grammar places the preposition at the end of a clause (stranding) in wh-questions ('What are you looking for?'), relative clauses without 'that/which' ('the pen I wrote with'), passive constructions ('The baby was looked after'), and infinitive post-modifiers ('a safe place to live in').
steps.simpleExplanation:
Master these rules from Assam's 'Position of Prepositions' and Odisha/Punjab preposition usage:
1) Natural End-Position: In everyday questions, say 'Who are you waiting for?' (very formal: 'For whom are you waiting?'). Never duplicate the preposition (*For whom are you waiting for? — wrong!). Never add 'to' after 'Where are you going?' (*Where are you going to? — avoid!).
2) Relative Clauses: Both 'the house in which she lives' (formal) and 'the house (that) she lives in' (natural) are grammatical; NEVER write *the house in that she lives (prepositions CANNOT precede 'that'!).
3) High-Scoring Collocations (Verb/Adjective/Noun + Fixed Preposition): 'good AT maths' (NOT *in), 'afraid OF', 'fond OF', 'interested IN', 'proud OF', 'depend ON', 'listen TO', 'congratulate someone ON' (NOT *for), 'prefer tea TO coffee' (NOT *than), 'accused OF', 'abstain FROM', 'cope WITH' (NEVER *cope up with!).

structurePatterns.formula: Wh-Question | Contact Relative Clause | Passive Verb + Preposition
structurePatterns.sample: What are you staring at? / That is the stool he stood on. / The plan was agreed on.

structurePatterns.formula: congratulate ON • good AT • prefer X TO Y • cope WITH • abstain FROM • consist OF
structurePatterns.sample: I congratulated Riya on her medal; she prefers chess to carrom.

realLifeExamples.sentence: This is the quiet bench that Grandfather always sits on—never write *on that he sits.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Preposition 'on' moves to the end when 'that' is used or omitted; *on that is ungrammatical.

realLifeExamples.sentence: She is remarkably good at geometry and knows how to cope with exam pressure.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: I congratulated him for his prize, though he prefers cricket than football and is weak in swimming.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: I congratulated him on his prize, though he prefers cricket to football and is weak at swimming.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Standard collocations require 'congratulate ON', 'prefer X TO Y', and 'good/weak AT' (or 'weak in a subject' vs 'at an activity', though 'weak at/in' vs 'good at' is standard).

exceptions: 'Die of' a disease/hunger ('died of malaria') vs. 'die from' an external cause/injury ('died from a snakebite / overwork').
'Angry WITH a person' vs. 'angry AT a thing/behaviour' ('angry with Chikoo at his carelessness').

steps.storyPrompt: Acharya Vidyadhar examines four ways to describe the missing diamond's velvet box.
steps.questionPrompt: Which sentence places the preposition grammatically?
options: Here is the velvet box in that the diamond was kept.
Here is the velvet box that the diamond was kept in.
Here is the velvet box in which the diamond was kept in.
Here is the velvet box which the diamond was kept.
acceptedAnswers: Here is the velvet box that the diamond was kept in.
steps.hint: Remember: a preposition CANNOT sit directly before 'that' (*in that), must NOT be repeated twice (*in which... in), and cannot be dropped completely!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Vault lock #3 unlocked! With 'that' (or omitted pronoun), 'in' goes neatly at the end ('that the diamond was kept in')."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Check three rules: never *in that, never double prepositions, and don't drop 'in'.

feedbackWrongByOption.Here is the velvet box in that the diamo: Prepositions can precede 'which' ('in which'), NEVER 'that' (*in that)!
feedbackWrongByOption.Here is the velvet box in which the diam: Doubles 'in' at both start and end!

steps.simplerExample: The pen that I write with (OR: the pen with which I write).

steps.storyPrompt: Chikoo reads the final vault inscription: "We prevented the thief to escape, and everyone congratulated Ira for her success!"
steps.questionPrompt: Pick the sentence that fixes BOTH preposition errors accurately:
options: We prevented the thief from escaping, and everyone congratulated Ira on her success!
We prevented the thief to escaping, and everyone congratulated Ira on her success!
We prevented the thief from escape, and everyone congratulated Ira for her success!
We prevented the thief against escaping, and everyone congratulated Ira at her success!
acceptedAnswers: We prevented the thief from escaping, and everyone congratulated Ira on her success!
steps.hint: 'Prevent someone FROM + V-ing', and 'congratulate someone ON + achievement'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "The Royal Diamond gleams again! 'Prevent... from + V-ing' and 'congratulate... on' are locked into treasure memory."

feedbackWrongByOption.We prevented the thief from escape, and: After preposition 'from', use gerund 'escaping', and 'congratulate' takes 'on'!

steps.simplerExample: Rain prevented us from playing; Mother congratulated me on my grades.

steps.settingDescription: Inside the velvet box behind the fourth pillar, Detective Ira lifts the sparkling diamond back onto Maharaj Vakya's cushion!

dialogues.line: Safe and sound! Right inside the velvet box that the crown jewel rests in—not a stray preposition out of place.
Check your Grammar Notebook for key preposition collocations and prove your detective instincts in the 15-question assessment.

steps.storyCallout: Module 18 Story Complete! Open your Grammar Notebook or try the Final Assessment.

summaryRules.heading: Time Pyramid & Space Contrasts
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Use AT for exact clock times/noon/night, ON for days/dates, IN for months/years/seasons/parts of day (except 'at night'). Use SINCE + point, FOR + duration; BY = deadline, UNTIL = duration up to.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: at 5 p.m. • on Monday • in July • since 2020 (point) vs for 3 years (length)
summaryRules.example: Wait here until noon; submit the report by Friday.

summaryRules.heading: Prepositional Objects & Zero-Preposition Verbs
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Follow prepositions with objective pronouns (me, him, them) and gerunds (-ing). Omit prepositions after direct transitive verbs like discuss, order, enter (a place), resemble, and marry.
summaryRules.example: We discussed the riddle calmly; heavy rain prevented us from leaving.

summaryRules.heading: Position of Prepositions & Core Collocations
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Prepositions stand at the end in natural wh-questions, contact relative clauses ('the chair I sat on'), and passives. Never place a preposition before 'that' (*in that). Key collocations: congratulate ON, prefer X TO Y, cope WITH, good AT.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: the house in which she lives = the house (that) she lives in (NEVER *in that)
summaryRules.example: Who are you waiting for? She is very good at chess and prefers it to cards.

memoryAids: Time Pyramid: AT = sharp tip (5 p.m.), ON = calendar square (Monday), IN = big box (August / 2026); drop ALL prepositions before 'today, yesterday, tomorrow, next/last + day'!
After ANY preposition (in, on, at, of, from, with, to as prep), verbs MUST wear '-ing'!

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: We will discuss about this on tomorrow and cope up with the delay.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: We will discuss this tomorrow and cope with the delay.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Do not add 'about' after 'discuss', 'on' before 'tomorrow', or 'up' inside 'cope with'.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: I prefer tea than coffee, and she insisted to go home.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: I prefer tea to coffee, and she insisted on going home.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Prefer' pairs with 'to' (not 'than'), and 'insist' takes preposition 'on' + gerund ('going').

exceptions: Note 'made of' (material unchanged: 'made of wood') vs. 'made from' (material transformed: 'cheese made from milk').
'Enter into' IS valid for non-physical agreements/conversations ('enter into an agreement'), though NOT for physical rooms ('enter the classroom').
textbookNotes: Consolidated across Assam Ch. 14 (Position of Prepositions), Punjab IX Ch. 3 (Prepositions), and Odisha X Ch. 5 (Prepositions).

questions.questionText: Fill in cleanly: "The science fair opens ____ 9:30 a.m. ____ Saturday ____ November."
options: on / at / in
at / on / in
in / on / at
at / in / on
questions.explanation: Clock time takes 'at' (at 9:30 a.m.), weekday takes 'on' (on Saturday), and month takes 'in' (in November).
questions.grammarRule: Use 'at' for clock times, 'on' for days/dates, and 'in' for months/seasons/years.

questions.questionText: Choose the right preposition pair: "Acharya has taught here ____ 2014, and Vaani has studied here ____ four years."
options: for / since
since / for
from / since
since / from
questions.explanation: With perfect tenses, 'since' marks a starting point (2014) and 'for' marks a length/duration (four years).
distractorRationales: 'From' does not pair with Present Perfect without 'to/until'.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'since + point in time' and 'for + period/duration of time'.

questions.questionText: Select the option matching this meaning: 'Submit your form no later than 4 p.m., because the desk stays open continuously up to 4 p.m.'
options: Submit it until 4 p.m.; the desk stays open by 4 p.m.
Submit it by 4 p.m.; the desk stays open until 4 p.m.
Submit it since 4 p.m.; the desk stays open for 4 p.m.
Submit it at 4 p.m.; the desk stays open on 4 p.m.
questions.explanation: 'By' marks a deadline (no later than); 'until' marks continuous duration up to a point.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'by' for a single deadline and 'until/till' for an activity continuing up to a time.

questions.questionText: Complete cleanly: "____ singing classically, Meera sat ____ her sister during the prize distribution."
options: Beside / besides
Besides / beside
Between / besides
Beside / among
questions.explanation: 'Besides' means 'in addition to' (+ gerund 'singing'); 'beside' means 'next to / by the side of'.
questions.grammarRule: 'Beside' = at the side of; 'besides' = in addition to / apart from.

questions.subtopicTitle: Position of prepositions in relative clauses
questions.questionText: Which sentence handles the preposition accurately inside a relative clause?
options: That is the wooden bridge on that we met yesterday.
That is the wooden bridge which we met on yesterday.
That is the wooden bridge on which we met on yesterday.
That is the wooden bridge that we met yesterday.
questions.explanation: Putting 'on' at the end ('which we met on') is grammatical; *on that is forbidden, *on which... on duplicates 'on', and dropping 'on' leaves 'met the bridge'.
distractorRationales: Never place a preposition immediately before 'that'.
Correct: preposition stranded cleanly at the end of the relative clause.
Omits required 'on' ('we met on the bridge').
questions.grammarRule: Never place a preposition before 'that'; strand it at the end or use 'preposition + which/whom'.

questions.questionText: Fill in accurately: "Good sportsmanship prevented the losing team ____ complaining ____ the referee's decision."
options: to / on
from / about
against / for
of / into
questions.explanation: 'Prevent [someone] from + V-ing' and 'complain about [something]' are standard collocations.
questions.grammarRule: Prepositions require nouns, object pronouns, or gerunds ('prevent from going', 'succeed in winning').

questions.questionText: Spot the sentence WITHOUT an extra/unnecessary preposition:
options: They discussed about the monsoon timetable.
He entered into the library quietly.
Her handwriting resembles her elder sister's.
We ordered for four masala dosas.
questions.explanation: 'Resemble', 'discuss', 'enter (a room)', and 'order (food)' take direct objects without prepositions (*resemble with/to, *discuss about, *enter into a room, *order for).
questions.grammarRule: Discuss, order, enter (a room), resemble, and await take direct objects with zero preposition.

questions.questionText: Choose the traditional distinction: "Years ago, many villagers died ____ cholera, while one traveller died ____ a severe snakebite."
options: from / of
of / from
with / by
by / of
questions.explanation: Standard grammar distinguishes 'die OF' a disease/hunger/thirst vs. 'die FROM' an injury, wound, or external cause.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'die of' for diseases/starvation and 'die from' for wounds, bites, or external causes.

questions.subtopicTitle: Prefer X to Y & Congratulate on
questions.questionText: Choose the accurate collocations: "She prefers classical music ____ pop, and we congratulated her ____ winning."
options: than / for
to / on
over / about
from / at
questions.explanation: Always say 'prefer A TO B' (never *prefer A than B) and 'congratulate someone ON' (standard exam collocation).
questions.grammarRule: Use 'prefer X to Y' and 'congratulate [person] on [achievement]'.

questions.questionText: Select the sentence using 'between' or 'among' accurately:
options: Divide the four prize books between the six winners.
Keep this map secret among you and me.
A direct bus runs between Kolkata, Bhubaneswar, and Puri.
She walked between the dense crowd alone.
questions.explanation: 'Between' applies to two items OR distinct named points viewed individually ('between Kolkata, Bhubaneswar, and Puri'), whereas undifferentiated groups of 3+ take 'among'.
distractorRationales: Six winners as a group take 'among'.
Correct: distinct named geographical points take 'between'.
Moving inside a single mass crowd takes 'through' or 'among'.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'between' for two or distinct individual entities, and 'among' for three or more as a group.

questions.questionText: Fill in both blanks accurately: "This flute is made ____ bamboo, whereas fine writing paper is made ____ bamboo pulp."
options: from / of
of / from
by / with
with / by
questions.explanation: Use 'made of' when the raw material stays recognisable ('flute made of bamboo'), and 'made from' when it undergoes chemical/physical transformation ('paper made from pulp').
questions.grammarRule: 'Made of' = original material remains visible; 'made from' = material is transformed.

options: He knows how to cope up with sudden power cuts.
The coach was angry with the goalkeeper at his careless mistake.
She is married with a marine biologist.
We arrived to the station five minutes early.
questions.explanation: 'Angry WITH a person' and 'angry AT a thing/action' are standard. Note: never *cope up with (say 'cope with'), say 'married TO', and 'arrived AT the station'.
distractorRationales: Use 'arrived at' a station (or 'in' a city), never *arrived to.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'cope with', 'married to', 'arrive at/in', and 'angry with (person) / at (thing)'.

options: Our school sports meet begins on next Wednesday.
Our school sports meet begins next Wednesday.
I spoke to the librarian on yesterday.
Will you visit the lab in this evening?
questions.explanation: Omit prepositions ('on/in') directly before 'this, that, next, last, every' + time noun, and before 'today, yesterday, tomorrow'.
questions.grammarRule: Drop time prepositions before 'next, last, this, every' + time word and before 'today/tomorrow/yesterday'.

questions.questionText: Which question avoids duplicating or misusing a preposition?
options: Where are you coming from?
Where are you going to?
For whom are you looking for?
With who did you travel with?
questions.explanation: 'Where are you coming from?' properly places 'from' at the end once; 'Where are you going?' needs no 'to'; C and D repeat prepositions twice.
distractorRationales: Avoid redundant 'to' in 'Where are you going?'.
questions.grammarRule: Never repeat a fronted preposition at the end of the same question.

questions.storyContext: Detective Ira logs the closing entry in the Treasury casebook.
questions.questionText: What is the exact difference between "The express train arrived ON time" and "We reached the platform just IN time to board"?
options: 'On time' means punctual (exact schedule); 'in time' means early enough before it is too late.
'In time' means punctual; 'on time' means barely catching the train.
Both phrases have identical meanings and can always swap.
'On time' is ungrammatical.
questions.explanation: 'On time' = exactly at the scheduled hour (punctual); 'in time' = before a deadline or before missing an opportunity.
questions.grammarRule: 'On time' = punctual as scheduled; 'in time' = soon enough before a cutoff.
